title: Short Stuff: Byford Dolphin Incident
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1983 Byford Dolphin diving accident in the North Sea. The hosts explain saturation diving, where divers live in pressurized chambers on a ship and travel to the seabed in a pressurized diving bell, so they decompress only once at the end of a multi-week hitch. They then describe the November 5 incident, in which a dive tender unclamped the diving bell from the trunk before the hatch was shut, causing a decompression explosion that killed four divers. They discuss the gruesome injuries, the lack of fear or pain, the regulatory response from the Norwegian Petroleum Directorate and Det Norske Veritas requiring retrofits and fail-safes, the original finding of human error, and later claims that the equipment was faulty. They close by crediting sources including a History Channel program and a Reddit post.

segments.title: Introduction and content warning
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and warns listeners that the story is graphic, involving people dying and being mutilated. He names the Byford Dolphin drilling rig, contracted by BP, and the November accident in the North Sea.

segments.title: What is saturation diving
segments.summary: The hosts explain saturation diving. Divers work hundreds of feet down and would otherwise need hours of daily decompression, so they live under pressure on a ship, travel to the seabed in a pressurized diving bell, and decompress only once at the end of a multi-week hitch.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief break before the account of the accident.

segments.title: The November accident
segments.summary: On November 5, a team of four divers was working in the Frigg gas field. A dive tender unclamped the diving bell from the trunk before the hatch was shut. The chambers at nine atmospheres were exposed to one atmosphere in under a second, causing an explosion that killed all four divers and the dive tender.

segments.title: Injuries, aftermath, and investigation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the injuries, including the diver closest to the door being torn apart, and say the deaths were instant with no pain or fear. They discuss the regulatory response requiring retrofits and fail-safes, the original finding of human error and fatigue, and later family claims that the equipment was faulty.

segments.title: Sources and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts credit a History Channel program and a Reddit post explaining saturation diving and the accident, then sign off.
